name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMAN_HEALTH_AND_DISEASE_STATEMENT_BASED_Q06 - Cellular transformation in cancer and retroviral HIV

questiontext.text:
Given below are five statements regarding cellular transformation in cancer and the pathogenesis of retroviral HIV infection:

(a) Normal animal cells show contact inhibition, a regulatory property that inhibits uncontrolled cell growth, whereas cancer cells appear to have lost this property.

(b) Malignant tumors remain strictly localized at their original tissue site and do not spread to distant anatomical organs.

(c) Following entry into macrophages, the single-stranded RNA genome of HIV is converted into viral DNA by the enzyme reverse transcriptase.

(d) Macrophages act as an HIV factory by continuously producing new viral particles without being immediately lysed.

(e) The progressive replication of HIV leads to a selective depletion of cytotoxic CD8+ T-lymphocytes while keeping helper CD4+ T-lymphocyte counts unchanged.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

कैंसर में कोशिकीय रूपांतरण और पश्चविषाणु (रेट्रोवायरस) एचआईवी संक्रमण के रोगजनन के संबंध में नीचे पाँच कथन दिए गए हैं:

(a) सामान्य जंतु कोशिकाएं संस्पर्श संदमन (कॉन्टैक्ट इनहिबिशन) प्रदर्शित करती हैं, जो अनियंत्रित कोशिका वृद्धि को रोकता है, जबकि कैंसर कोशिकाएं इस गुण को खो देती हैं।

(b) दुर्दम (मैलिग्नेंट) अर्बुद अपने मूल ऊतक स्थल पर ही सीमित रहते हैं और दूर के शारीरिक अंगों में नहीं फैलते हैं।

(c) मैक्रोफेज में प्रवेश के बाद, एचआईवी का एकल-रज्जुक आरएनए जीनोम रिवर्स ट्रांसक्रिप्टेज़ एंजाइम द्वारा वायरल डीएनए में बदल जाता है।

(d) मैक्रोफेज तुरंत नष्ट हुए बिना लगातार नए विषाणु कणों का उत्पादन करके एचआईवी कारखाने के रूप में कार्य करते हैं।

(e) एचआईवी का निरंतर प्रतिकृतियन साइटोटॉक्सिक CD8+ टी-लसीकाणुओं की संख्या में भारी कमी करता है, जबकि सहायक CD4+ टी-लसीकाणुओं की संख्या को अपरिवर्तित रखता है।

नीचे दिए गए विकल्पों में से सही उत्तर चुनें:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principles of Oncogenic Transformation and Retroviral Pathogenesis
Oncogenesis involves breakdown of strict homeostatic cell cycle restraints such as contact inhibition, while lentiviral retroviruses exploit cellular machinery to integrate proviral DNA and systematically ablate helper immune compartments.

Step 2: Evaluation of Cellular Contact Inhibition in Neoplasia
Normal cells cease division upon physical contact with neighboring cells, maintaining monolayer architecture; malignant transformation abolishes this contact inhibition, prompting continuous proliferation into disorganized tumor masses.

Step 3: Evaluation of Neoplastic Invasiveness and Metastatic Dissemination
Benign tumors remain confined to their primary site, but malignant neoplasms invade adjacent stroma, enter lymphatic and vascular channels, and establish secondary colonies at distant sites through metastasis, the most dreaded hallmark of cancer.

Step 4: Evaluation of Retroviral Reverse Transcription in Host Monocytes
Upon viral penetration into host macrophages, the retroviral reverse transcriptase enzyme transcribes viral genomic single-stranded RNA into complementary double-stranded DNA, which integrates into the host chromosome via viral integrase.

Step 5: Evaluation of Macrophage Reservoir and Viral Production
Infected macrophages transcribe and assemble new virions continuously without undergoing immediate cytolysis, functioning as durable long-term reservoirs and viral factories during HIV infection.

Step 6: Evaluation of Helper T-Cell Depletion and Immunodeficiency
HIV progeny specifically target, infect, and lyse helper CD4+ T-lymphocytes, causing a progressive and profound drop in CD4+ counts below 200 cells per microliter, inducing susceptibility to opportunistic pathogens; it does not selectively destroy CD8+ cells while sparing CD4+ cells.

Step 7: Final Conceptual Conclusion
The facts concerning loss of contact inhibition in malignant transformation, reverse transcription in macrophages, and the macrophage viral factory role are scientifically established, whereas asserting that malignant tumors do not metastasize and that HIV spares CD4+ T-cells while destroying CD8+ T-cells are biologically false. Consequently, only the propositions regarding contact inhibition loss, reverse transcription, and macrophage viral generation are accurate.

चरण 1: कैंसर रूपांतरण और रेट्रोवायरल रोगजनन के सिद्धांत
कैंसरजनन में संस्पर्श संदमन जैसी सामान्य नियंत्रण प्रणालियों का ह्रास होता है, जबकि एचआईवी जैसे रेट्रोवायरस पोषद कोशिकाओं का उपयोग करके अपनी संख्या बढ़ाते हैं और सहायक प्रतिरक्षा तंत्र को नष्ट करते हैं।

चरण 2: कैंसर कोशिकाओं में संस्पर्श संदमन के ह्रास का मूल्यांकन
सामान्य कोशिकाएं संस्पर्श संदमन का गुण प्रदर्शित करती हैं, जिससे अन्य कोशिकाओं के संपर्क में आने पर उनकी अनियंत्रित वृद्धि रुक जाती है; कैंसर कोशिकाएं इस गुण को खो देती हैं और विभाजित होकर गांठ या अर्बुद बना लेती हैं।

चरण 3: अर्बुद की आक्रामकता और मेटास्टेसिस का मूल्यांकन
सुदम (सौम्य) अर्बुद अपने मूल स्थान तक सीमित रहते हैं, जबकि दुर्दम (घातक) अर्बुद तेजी से बढ़ते हैं, आस-पास के सामान्य ऊतकों पर हमला करते हैं और रक्त द्वारा शरीर के दूर-दराज के अंगों में फैलकर नए ट्यूमर बनाते हैं (मेटास्टेसिस)।

चरण 4: मैक्रोफेज में रिवर्स ट्रांसक्रिप्शन का मूल्यांकन
मैक्रोफेज में प्रवेश करने पर, एचआईवी का आरएनए जीनोम रिवर्स ट्रांसक्रिप्टेज़ एंजाइम की मदद से वायरल डीएनए में बदल जाता है, जो बाद में पोषद कोशिका के डीएनए में जुड़ जाता है।

चरण 5: एचआईवी कारखाने के रूप में मैक्रोफेज का मूल्यांकन
संक्रमित मैक्रोफेज तुरंत नष्ट हुए बिना लगातार नए वायरस कणों का उत्पादन करते रहते हैं, जिससे वे शरीर में वायरस निर्माण के प्रमुख कारखाने की तरह कार्य करते हैं।

चरण 6: सहायक टी-कोशिकाओं के ह्रास का मूल्यांकन
एचआईवी विशेष रूप से सहायक CD4+ टी-लसीकाणुओं पर हमला करता है और उन्हें नष्ट करता है, जिससे शरीर में CD4+ कोशिकाओं की संख्या तेजी से घट जाती है और रोगी अवसरवादी संक्रमणों का शिकार हो जाता है; यह CD8+ कोशिकाओं को चुनिंदा रूप से नष्ट नहीं करता।

चरण 7: अंतिम वैचारिक निष्कर्ष
कैंसर में संस्पर्श संदमन की समाप्ति, मैक्रोफेज में रिवर्स ट्रांसक्रिप्शन और मैक्रोफेज के एचआईवी कारखाने के रूप में कार्य करने के विवरण सत्य हैं, जबकि दुर्दम ट्यूमर के सीमित रहने और CD4+ कोशिकाओं के अप्रभावित रहने के दावे असत्य हैं। अतः केवल संस्पर्श संदमन ह्रास, रिवर्स ट्रांसक्रिप्शन और मैक्रोफेज कारखाने से संबंधित कथन ही सत्य हैं।

answer.text: Statements (a), (b), and (c) only
Statements (a), (c), and (d) only
Statements (b), (d), and (e) only
Statements (a), (c), and (e) only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMAN_HEALTH_AND_DISEASE_MATCHING_Q01 - Match infectious pathogens with their respective diseases

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Pathogen) List II (Disease)
A. Salmonella typhi I. Pneumonia
B. Streptococcus pneumoniae II. Amoebiasis
C. Entamoeba histolytica III. Ringworm
D. Microsporum IV. Typhoid

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the disease caused by Salmonella typhi
Salmonella typhi is a pathogenic bacterium that enters the human small intestine through contaminated food and water and migrates to other organs via blood, causing typhoid fever characterized by sustained high fever, weakness, and stomach pain.

Step 2: Identify the disease caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae infect the alveoli of the lungs, causing fluid accumulation that leads to respiratory difficulties typical of pneumonia.

Step 3: Identify the disease caused by Entamoeba histolytica
Entamoeba histolytica is an intestinal protozoan parasite that infects the large intestine of humans, causing amoebiasis or amoebic dysentery, marked by abdominal cramps and stools with excess mucus and blood clots.

Step 4: Identify the disease caused by Microsporum
Microsporum, along with Trichophyton and Epidermophyton, is a fungal genus responsible for ringworm, a contagious disease presenting as dry, scaly, intensely itchy lesions on skin, nails, and scalp.

Step 5: Verify the complete conceptual pairing
Matching each pathogen to its corresponding human disease establishes the correct pairings: Salmonella typhi pairs with Typhoid, Streptococcus pneumoniae pairs with Pneumonia, Entamoeba histolytica pairs with Amoebiasis, and Microsporum pairs with Ringworm. Thus, A corresponds to IV, B corresponds to I, C corresponds to II, and D corresponds to III.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMAN_HEALTH_AND_DISEASE_MATCHING_Q02 - Match innate immunity barriers with their examples

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Innate Defence Barrier) List II (Biological Component/Example)
A. Physical barriers I. Polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNL) and monocytes
B. Physiological barriers II. Interferons
C. Cellular barriers III. Skin and mucus coating of mucosal epithelium
D. Cytokine barriers IV. Hydrochloric acid in stomach, saliva, and tears

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze physical barriers of innate immunity
Physical barriers provide an anatomical obstacle against microbial entry; the skin on our body forms the primary external barrier, while the mucus coating of the epithelium lining the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and urogenital tracts traps invading microorganisms.

Step 2: Analyze physiological barriers of innate immunity
Physiological barriers involve chemical secretions and physiological conditions that inhibit microbial growth, such as the low pH of stomach acid, lysozyme and antibacterial agents in saliva in the mouth, and tears from the eyes.

Step 3: Analyze cellular barriers of innate immunity
Cellular barriers consist of specialized phagocytic white blood cells in blood and tissues, including polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNL-neutrophils), monocytes, natural killer lymphocytes, and tissue macrophages that engulf and destroy microbes.

Step 4: Analyze cytokine barriers of innate immunity
Cytokine barriers comprise soluble signalling glycoproteins like interferons, which are secreted by virus-infected host cells to protect neighboring uninfected cells from further viral replication.

Step 5: Verify the complete conceptual pairing
Associating each category of barrier with its accurate representative example yields: Physical barriers pair with Skin and mucus coating of mucosal epithelium; Physiological barriers pair with Hydrochloric acid in stomach, saliva, and tears; Cellular barriers pair with Polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNL) and monocytes; and Cytokine barriers pair with Interferons. Hence, A corresponds to III, B corresponds to IV, C corresponds to I, and D corresponds to II.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMAN_HEALTH_AND_DISEASE_MATCHING_Q03 - Match clinical immunisation scenarios with immunity types

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Clinical Scenario) List II (Type of Immunity)
A. Ingestion of maternal colostrum rich in IgA by a neonate I. Artificially acquired active immunity
B. Administration of preformed antitoxin antibodies following a rusty nail injury II. Naturally acquired passive immunity
C. Inoculation of inactivated or weakened antigenic pathogens during vaccination III. Naturally acquired active immunity
D. Antibody generation following recovery from a natural wild viral infection IV. Artificially acquired passive immunity

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate immunity acquired via colostrum
Colostrum secreted during the early days of lactation provides preformed maternal secretory IgA antibodies directly to the nursing infant without requiring the infant's own immune system to respond actively. Because this transfer occurs biologically without medical intervention, it represents naturally acquired passive immunity.

Step 2: Evaluate immunity from direct injection of antitoxin
In cases requiring immediate neutralisation of deadly toxins, such as tetanus, preformed antibodies or antitoxin preparations are directly administered into the patient. Because readymade antibodies are medically introduced from an external source, it represents artificially acquired passive immunity.

Step 3: Evaluate immunity stimulated by vaccines
Vaccination introduces weakened, killed, or antigenic components of a pathogen into an individual, stimulating the recipient's own B and T lymphocytes to produce memory cells and antibodies. Because the host body actively manufactures the response following clinical inoculation, it constitutes artificially acquired active immunity.

Step 4: Evaluate immunity following natural illness
When a living pathogen naturally infects an individual, the host's immune cells encounter the foreign antigens directly and mount a primary immune response, resulting in active antibody and memory cell generation. This constitutes naturally acquired active immunity.

Step 5: Verify the complete conceptual pairing
Connecting each clinical case to its precise classification shows: Ingestion of colostrum pairs with Naturally acquired passive immunity; Administration of preformed antitoxin pairs with Artificially acquired passive immunity; Inoculation of weakened pathogens pairs with Artificially acquired active immunity; and Antibody generation following natural infection pairs with Naturally acquired active immunity. Therefore, A corresponds to II, B corresponds to IV, C corresponds to I, and D corresponds to III.

Step 1: Clarify the principle and use of the Widal test
The Widal test is a standard serological procedure used specifically in clinical medicine to confirm typhoid fever caused by Salmonella typhi.

Step 2: Clarify the principle and use of ELISA
Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) functions on the principle of specific antigen-antibody interaction and serves as a primary diagnostic screening test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV/AIDS) infection.

Step 3: Clarify the principle and use of biopsy and histopathological examination
In a biopsy, a piece of suspected cancerous tissue is excised, sliced into thin sections, stained, and subjected to microscopic histopathological analysis by a pathologist to detect neoplastic cell changes.

Step 4: Clarify the principle and use of MRI
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) utilizes strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations to safely and accurately detect physiological and pathological alterations in deep soft tissues without exposing the patient to X-rays.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMAN_HEALTH_AND_DISEASE_MATCHING_Q06 - Match human diseases with their classic symptoms

questiontext.text:

B. Elephantiasis (Filariasis) II. Dry, scaly circular lesions with intense itching on skin, nails, or scalp

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify characteristic symptoms of ascariasis
Ascaris lumbricoides is an intestinal roundworm parasite that proliferates in the gut, causing internal bleeding, muscular pain, persistent fever, anemia, and physical blockage of the intestinal lumen.

Step 2: Identify characteristic symptoms of elephantiasis
Wuchereria bancrofti and Wuchereria malayi live inside the lymphatic system for many years, producing slowly developing chronic inflammation of the lymphatic vessels, predominantly in the lower extremities and genital organs, resulting in gross deformities.

Step 3: Identify characteristic symptoms of ringworm
Dermatophytic fungal infections of the genera Microsporum, Trichophyton, and Epidermophyton lead to localized dry, scaly skin lesions accompanied by intense pruritus (itching), particularly in moisture-retaining body folds.

Step 4: Identify characteristic symptoms of amoebiasis
Infection by the protozoan Entamoeba histolytica damages the mucosal lining of the large intestine, causing constipation, severe abdominal cramps, and frequent passage of stools accompanied by excess mucus and dark blood clots.

Step 5: Verify the complete conceptual pairing
Connecting each clinical disease condition to its diagnostic manifestation confirms: Ascariasis pairs with Internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anemia, and intestinal blockage; Elephantiasis pairs with Chronic inflammation of lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs and genital deformities; Ringworm pairs with Dry, scaly circular lesions with intense itching on skin, nails, or scalp; and Amoebiasis pairs with Stools with excess mucus and blood clots with abdominal cramps. name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMAN_HEALTH_AND_DISEASE_MATCHING_Q07 - Match lymphoid organs with their structural functions

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

B. Thymus II. Bean-shaped organ filtering blood-borne microbes and serving as an erythrocyte reservoir

D. Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) IV. Primary lymphoid organ where all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine the role of bone marrow
Bone marrow is the primary central lymphoid organ responsible for the synthesis of all cellular blood elements, including the generation and early differentiation of both B and T lymphocytes.

Step 2: Determine the role of the thymus
The thymus is a primary lobed lymphoid organ positioned near the heart and beneath the sternum (breastbone); it provides the essential micro-environment for T-lymphocyte maturation and progressively atrophies, becoming quite small by puberty.

Step 3: Determine the role of the spleen
The spleen is a large, secondary bean-shaped lymphoid organ containing phagocytes and lymphocytes; it filters peripheral circulation by trapping blood-borne pathogens and acts as a major reservoir of erythrocytes.

Step 4: Determine the role of MALT
Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) is strategically located within the mucosal linings of major internal passages (respiratory, digestive, and urogenital tracts) and accounts for approximately 50 percent of all lymphoid tissue in the human body.

Step 5: Verify the complete conceptual pairing
Associating each lymphoid structure with its key physiological characteristic yields: Bone marrow pairs with Primary lymphoid organ where all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced; Thymus pairs with Lobed organ located beneath breastbone that steadily reduces in size with age; Spleen pairs with Bean-shaped organ filtering blood-borne microbes and serving as an erythrocyte reservoir; and MALT pairs with Constitutes roughly 50 percent of the lymphoid tissue in the human body. Thus, A corresponds to IV, B corresponds to III, C corresponds to II, and D corresponds to I.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMAN_HEALTH_AND_DISEASE_MATCHING_Q08 - Match Plasmodium developmental stages with their events

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Stage/Product in Plasmodium Life Cycle) List II (Biological Event and Site)
A. Sporozoites I. Toxic substance released upon rupture of RBCs causing recurring chills and high fever
B. Haemozoin II. Sexual fertilization and zygotic development occurring inside mosquito gut
C. Gametocytes III. Motile infectious forms stored in mosquito salivary glands that initiate human infection
D. Syngamy and sporogony IV. Sexual stages developing within red blood cells of the human host

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the nature and function of sporozoites
Sporozoites represent the mature, motile infectious forms of Plasmodium that reside in the salivary glands of the female Anopheles mosquito; they are inoculated into the human bloodstream during a mosquito bite to initiate hepatic infection.

Step 2: Identify the origin and pathological action of haemozoin
Haemozoin is a toxic, crystalline byproduct released into circulation when infected host erythrocytes burst synchronously, directly triggering the paroxysms of severe chills and high fever recurring every 3 to 4 days.

Step 3: Identify the site of gametocyte development
Asexual erythrocytic schizogony eventually gives rise to sexual precursor cells, the male and female gametocytes, which differentiate within human red blood cells and await ingestion by a female Anopheles vector during a blood meal.

Step 4: Identify where syngamy and sporogonic development occur
Once ingested by the mosquito vector, microgametes and macrogametes undergo fertilization in the mosquito's gut lumen, developing into motile ookinetes, oocysts, and ultimately generating sporozoites that migrate to the salivary glands.

Step 5: Verify the complete conceptual pairing
Relating each stage of the malarial life cycle to its exact developmental event establishes: Sporozoites pair with Motile infectious forms stored in mosquito salivary glands that initiate human infection; Haemozoin pairs with Toxic substance released upon rupture of RBCs causing recurring chills and high fever; Gametocytes pair with Sexual stages developing within red blood cells of the human host; and Syngamy and sporogony pair with Sexual fertilization and zygotic development occurring inside mosquito gut. Thus, A corresponds to III, B corresponds to I, C corresponds to IV, and D corresponds to II.

D. Nicotine IV. Interferes with neurotransmitter dopamine transport, producing CNS stimulation, euphoria, and hallucinations at high doses

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the physiological action of diacetylmorphine
Heroin or smack (chemically diacetylmorphine) binds specifically to opioid receptors in the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract, acting as a depressant that retards body functions and respiratory rate.

Step 2: Analyze the physiological action of cannabinoids
Cannabinoids interact directly with cannabinoid receptors distributed predominantly in brain tissue; when inhaled or ingested orally, they exert prominent physiological impacts on the human cardiovascular system.

Step 3: Analyze the physiological action of cocaine
Cocaine inhibits the reuptake of dopamine by interfering with dopamine transporters, thereby amplifying dopaminergic neurotransmission in the CNS, eliciting intense euphoria, heightened alertness, and hallucinations in excessive dosages.

Step 4: Analyze the physiological action of nicotine
Nicotine is a tobacco alkaloid that stimulates the adrenal glands to secrete adrenaline and nor-adrenaline into the blood, resulting in peripheral vasoconstriction, elevated arterial blood pressure, and increased heart rate.

Step 5: Verify the complete conceptual pairing
Linking each chemical compound with its documented neurochemical target demonstrates: Diacetylmorphine pairs with Acts as a depressant and slows body functions by binding opioid receptors in CNS and gut; Cannabinoids pair with Interacts with specific receptors in the brain, producing marked effects on the cardiovascular system; Cocaine pairs with Interferes with neurotransmitter dopamine transport, producing CNS stimulation, euphoria, and hallucinations at high doses; and Nicotine pairs with Stimulates adrenal medulla to release adrenaline, elevating arterial blood pressure and heart rate. name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMAN_HEALTH_AND_DISEASE_MATCHING_Q10 - Match oncology concepts with biological definitions

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Oncological Term/Agent) List II (Biological Definition / Characteristic Property)
A. Contact inhibition I. Biological response modifier administered to activate the host immune system to destroy tumors
B. Metastasis II. Normal cellular genes that can undergo activation under certain conditions to induce oncogenic transformation
C. Proto-oncogenes (c-onc) III. Regulatory property of normal cells where contact with neighboring cells suppresses uncontrolled division
D. \(\alpha\)-Interferon IV. Most feared property of malignant cells sloughing off to colonize distant body sites via the bloodstream

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define contact inhibition in cell biology
Contact inhibition is an intrinsic regulatory mechanism exhibited by normal eukaryotic cells, whereby physical contact with adjacent cells inhibits mitotic division; the breakdown or loss of this property is a hallmark of cancerous transformation.

Step 2: Define metastasis in malignant tumors
Metastasis is the defining and most lethal attribute of malignant neoplasms, in which proliferating neoplastic cells detach from the primary tumor mass, invade surrounding vessels, travel through blood or lymph, and establish secondary tumor foci at distant anatomical sites.

Step 3: Define proto-oncogenes
Proto-oncogenes (or cellular oncogenes, c-onc) are normal evolutionary conserved cellular genes regulating cell cycle progression; when mutated, rearranged, or improperly expressed due to carcinogenic agents, they convert into active oncogenes that drive neoplastic transformation.

Step 4: Define the role of \(\alpha\)-interferon in cancer immunotherapy
Tumor cells often evade immune surveillance and destruction. Biological response modifiers such as \(\alpha\)-interferon are clinically administered to patients to stimulate and activate their innate and cell-mediated immune responses to target and destroy tumor cells.

Step 5: Verify the complete conceptual pairing
Associating each oncological concept with its precise scientific description yields: Contact inhibition pairs with Regulatory property of normal cells where contact with neighboring cells suppresses uncontrolled division; Metastasis pairs with Most feared property of malignant cells sloughing off to colonize distant body sites via the bloodstream; Proto-oncogenes pairs with Normal cellular genes that can undergo activation under certain conditions to induce oncogenic transformation; and \(\alpha\)-Interferon pairs with Biological response modifier administered to activate the host immune system to destroy tumors. Thus, A corresponds to III, B corresponds to IV, C corresponds to II, and D corresponds to I.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMAN_HEALTH_AND_DISEASE_MCQ_Q01 - Sequence of events in retroviral replication

questiontext.text:
Consider the following events occurring during the replication and pathogenesis of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) inside a human host:

  1. Integration of the synthesized viral DNA into the host cell genome.
  2. Progressive reduction in the population of helper T-lymphocytes leading to opportunistic infections.
  3. Entry of viral RNA into host macrophages and its conversion into viral DNA by reverse transcriptase.
  4. Release of progeny virions into the bloodstream to attack circulating helper T-lymphocytes.

Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these events?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Retroviral Infection
Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is an enveloped retrovirus possessing a single-stranded RNA genome. Its pathogenesis in humans follows an orderly molecular and cellular cascade starting from primary viral entry and reverse transcription, through proviral genomic integration and viral progeny production, culminating in the destruction of cell-mediated immunity.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Chronological Evaluation
1. Initial Infection and Reverse Transcription: Upon gaining access to the body, HIV first enters antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages. Inside the macrophage cytoplasm, the viral RNA core serves as a template for the enzyme reverse transcriptase to synthesize complementary viral DNA.
2. Proviral Genomic Integration: The newly synthesized double-stranded viral DNA is transported into the host cell nucleus, where it incorporates into the host genome. The host cell is directed to transcribe viral genes, transforming macrophages into continuous producers of virus particles (functioning as an HIV factory).
3. Attack on Helper T-Lymphocytes: Progeny virions released from macrophages enter the bloodstream and selectively bind and enter helper T-lymphocytes (\(\mathrm{T_H}\)), where replication repeats.
4. Immune Depletion: Successive rounds of replication lead to a progressive decrease in the number of helper T-lymphocytes in the infected person. The resulting severe immunodeficiency renders the host vulnerable to life-threatening opportunistic pathogens, including Mycobacterium, Toxoplasma, fungi, and viruses.

Step 3: Verification of Event Ordering
The physiological sequence is unequivocally: conversion of viral RNA into viral DNA in macrophages, followed by incorporation of viral DNA into the host cell genome, followed by release of progeny virions to attack helper T-lymphocytes, and finally the progressive depletion of helper T-lymphocytes leading to opportunistic infections.

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Conclusion
Therefore, the correct chronological sequence is: (III) → (I) → (IV) → (II).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMAN_HEALTH_AND_DISEASE_MCQ_Q02 - Chronological stages of Plasmodium life cycle

questiontext.text:
The following events occur during the digenetic life cycle of the malarial parasite Plasmodium across human and mosquito hosts:

  1. Fertilization and zygote development within the gut wall of the female mosquito vector.
  2. Inoculation of motile sporozoites into the human bloodstream through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.
  3. Rupture of infected erythrocytes accompanied by the release of the toxic pigment haemozoin.
  4. Asexual multiplication of the parasite within human hepatocytes and release of merozoites into the blood.
  5. Development of sexual stages (gametocytes) within human red blood cells and their subsequent uptake during a mosquito blood meal.

Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these stages starting from a mosquito bite on a healthy human?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of the Digenetic Malarial Life Cycle
Plasmodium requires two hosts to complete its complex life cycle: humans (where asexual reproduction and gametocyte differentiation take place) and female Anopheles mosquitoes (where sexual fertilization and sporogony take place). The cycle proceeds in a defined anatomical and developmental progression.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Chronological Evaluation
1. Inoculation: When an infected female Anopheles bites a human, infective sporozoites stored in its salivary glands are injected into the peripheral circulation.
2. Pre-erythrocytic (Hepatic) Schizogony: Sporozoites reach the liver via blood within minutes, invade hepatocytes, and reproduce asexually, ultimately bursting the liver cells to release parasites into the bloodstream.
3. Erythrocytic Schizogony and Paroxysm: The released parasites invade red blood cells, reproducing asexually. The cyclic rupture of red blood cells releases new parasites along with haemozoin (a toxic byproduct of hemoglobin digestion), which induces recurring chills and high fever.
4. Gametocytogenesis and Ingestion: Within red blood cells, a subset of parasites differentiates into sexual forms called male and female gametocytes. When a female Anopheles mosquito feeds on the infected human, it takes up these gametocytes with its blood meal.
5. Fertilization and Sporogony in Mosquito: In the mosquito gut, gametocytes emerge and undergo fertilization. The resulting zygote develops into an ookinete, forms an oocyst on the gut wall, and undergoes sporogony to produce sporozoites that migrate to the salivary glands.

Step 3: Verification of Event Ordering
Tracing the complete cycle sequentially: introduction of sporozoites via mosquito bite occurs first, followed by asexual reproduction inside hepatocytes, followed by rupture of red blood cells with release of haemozoin, followed by formation and uptake of gametocytes, and finally syngamy and development inside the mosquito gut.

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Conclusion
Therefore, the correct chronological sequence is: (II) → (IV) → (III) → (V) → (I).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q01 - Agricultural research on crop variety improvement

generalfeedback.text:

At the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI), M.S. Swaminathan spearheaded initiatives in genetics and plant breeding to enhance crop productivity and food security.

Step 2: Identification of Specific Research Facility
The School of Cytogenetics and Radiation Research established at IARI provided the specialised institutional base where Swaminathan and his team developed short-duration, high-yielding rice varieties, including scented Basmati.

Step 3: Deduction of the Correct Institute
Other centers such as national dairy institutes, botanical surveys, or forestry institutes focus on different biological domains rather than cytogenetics and mutation breeding at IARI.

Final Answer: School of Cytogenetics and Radiation Research

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q02 - Experimental disproof of good humor hypothesis

questiontext.text: The 'good humor' hypothesis of health, which asserted that a person with 'blackbile' had a hot personality and suffered from fevers, was experimentally disproved by which scientist?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Foundation of Humoral Theory
Early medical systems, including Hippocratic and Ayurvedic traditions, postulated that health represents a balance of bodily humors, associating blackbile with elevated temperature and fever.

Step 2: Experimental Refutation
William Harvey revolutionized physiology by discovering blood circulation through rigorous experimental methods. Furthermore, he demonstrated that individuals possessing blackbile maintained normal body temperatures when measured with a clinical thermometer.

Step 3: Confirmation of Investigator
Harvey's physical measurements directly invalidated the speculative humor hypothesis in favor of experimental physiology.

Final Answer: William Harvey

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q03 - Factors influencing human health status

questiontext.text: According to principles of modern biology, human health is adversely affected by which triad of contributing factors?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Biological Definition of Health
Health represents a holistic state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being rather than merely an absence of clinical symptoms or physical fitness.

Step 2: Categorization of Deleterious Influences
Human health is influenced by three broad categories: genetic disorders inherited congenitally from parents, infections caused by communicable pathogens, and individual lifestyle factors including dietary habits, rest, and physical exercise.

Step 3: Assessment of Impact
All three parameters interact continuously to govern the physiological, psychological, and anatomical integrity of the individual.

Final Answer: Genetic disorders, infections, and individual lifestyle

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q04 - Survival adaptations of enteric human pathogens

questiontext.text: Enteric bacterial pathogens that successfully infect the human gastrointestinal tract must possess specific adaptations to overcome which primary physiological barriers of the stomach?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Physiological Defense of Gastric Juice
The human stomach acts as a formidable physiological barrier against microbial invasion by secreting highly acidic hydrochloric acid and potent proteolytic enzymes.

Step 2: Adaptive Mechanisms of Ingested Pathogens
To establish infection in the gut, enteric microbes must survive exposure to low pH conditions in the gastric lumen and resist enzymatic digestion by gastric and intestinal proteases.

Step 3: Conclusion on Enteric Survival
Without mechanisms to withstand profound gastric acidity and proteolytic degradation, ingested microbes are neutralized before colonizing the intestinal mucosa.

Final Answer: Low pH environment and resistance to digestive enzymes

Step 1: Pathogen Characteristics and Route
Salmonella typhi is a pathogenic bacterium causing typhoid enteric fever in humans, primarily transmitted through contaminated food and water.

Step 2: Site of Primary Invasion
Upon ingestion, the bacteria first enter the lumen and mucosal lining of the small intestine, from which they penetrate into the bloodstream to disseminate systemically.

Step 3: Clinical Confirmation
Initial colonization of the small intestine precedes bacteremia and subsequent invasion of secondary systemic organs.

Final Answer: Small intestine through contaminated food and water

questiontext.text: Which clinical serological test is routinely employed to confirm typhoid fever, famously spread for years by the asymptomatic carrier Mary Mallon?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical Case and Diagnostics
Mary Mallon, known as Typhoid Mary, was an asymptomatic chronic carrier who spread Salmonella typhi through the culinary items she prepared.

Step 2: Serological Assay Identification
Typhoid fever is diagnostically confirmed in laboratory medicine by the Widal test, an agglutination reaction detecting specific antibodies against Salmonella antigens.

Step 3: Differentiation from Other Tests
ELISA is standard for retroviral screening, biopsy for neoplasia, and Western blot for confirmatory protein detection.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q07 - Diagnostic signs and severe complications of typhoid

questiontext.text: Which combination of clinical manifestations is characteristic of acute typhoid fever, and what critical complication can lead to fatality in severe cases?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Clinical Presentation of Enteric Fever
Infection by Salmonella typhi is clinically marked by sustained high pyrexia reaching \(39^\circ\text{C}\) to \(40^\circ\text{C}\), profound weakness, abdominal pain, constipation, persistent headache, and loss of appetite.

Step 2: Pathological Progression and Complication
As the pathogen multiplies within intestinal lymphoid tissue, severe cases can lead to ulceration and intestinal perforation, accompanied by fatal peritonitis if left untreated.

Step 3: Distinction from Respiratory Illness
Fluid collection in pulmonary alveoli is characteristic of pneumonia, not enteric perforation seen in typhoid.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q08 - Etiological agents responsible for bacterial pneumonia

questiontext.text: Bacterial pneumonia in humans, which primarily infects the alveoli of the lungs, is caused by which group of pathogens?

Step 1: Target Site and Pathology
Pneumonia targets the respiratory gas-exchange units, specifically causing the air-filled alveolar sacs to become engorged with inflammatory fluid.

Step 2: Causative Microorganisms
The primary bacterial species responsible for human pneumonia are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae.

Step 3: Distinction from Viral and Enteric Agents
Rhino viruses cause upper respiratory tract infections, while Salmonella causes enteric fever and Entamoeba causes dysentery.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q09 - Pathophysiological features of severe pneumonia

questiontext.text: In severe, advanced cases of bacterial pneumonia, what physiological change causes the lips and fingernails to turn gray to bluish in colour?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Alveolar Consolidation Mechanism
Bacterial proliferation inside lung alveoli leads to intense exudation, filling the air-filled sacs with fluid and severely impairing oxygen diffusion across the respiratory membrane.

Step 2: Cyanosis Manifestation
The resulting hypoxemia and elevated levels of deoxygenated hemoglobin in peripheral microcirculation produce a distinctive gray to bluish discoloration (cyanosis) of peripheral extremities such as the lips and fingernails.

Step 3: Assessment of Peripheral Signs
This peripheral bluish tinge directly reflects acute failure of alveolar gas exchange rather than hemolysis or localized fungal infiltration.

Final Answer: Impaired gas exchange due to fluid accumulation in alveoli

questiontext.text: How does the infection caused by Rhino viruses in the common cold anatomically differ from bacterial pneumonia?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Anatomical Specificity of Rhino Viruses
Rhino viruses represent a primary etiological group causing the common cold, selectively infecting the nasal mucous membrane and upper respiratory passage.

Step 2: Comparison with Pneumonic Infection
Rhino viral pathology spares the lower respiratory tract, strictly avoiding infection of the pulmonary alveoli, whereas bacterial pneumonia directly compromises the alveolar sacs.

Step 3: Diagnostic Separation
Common cold is an upper respiratory infection lasting 3 to 7 days without alveolar exudation, providing a clear anatomical contrast to alveolar pneumonia.

questiontext.text: Among the different species of Plasmodium responsible for human malaria, which species causes malignant malaria that can be fatal?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Diversity of Malarial Parasites
Human malaria is caused by several protozoan species of the genus Plasmodium, including Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium malariae, and Plasmodium falciparum.

Step 2: Virulence and Severity
Plasmodium falciparum produces malignant tertian malaria, characterized by high parasite burdens, severe complications, vascular occlusion, and potential mortality.

Step 3: Designation of Species
While other species induce debilitating recurring fevers, malignant and frequently fatal malaria is specifically attributable to Plasmodium falciparum.

Final Answer: Plasmodium falciparum

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q12 - Toxin responsible for paroxysmal malarial fevers

questiontext.text: The recurring episodes of severe chills and high fever recurring every three to four days in malaria are triggered by the release of which substance during erythrocyte rupture?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Erythrocytic Schizogony
Within the human host, Plasmodium merozoites invade red blood cells, where they replicate asexually until the host erythrocytes rupture synchronously.

Step 2: Haemozoin Release and Action
Lysis of infected erythrocytes discharges parasite progeny along with haemozoin, a toxic crystalline byproduct of hemoglobin breakdown, which triggers pyrogenic release inducing shaking chills and paroxysmal high fever.

Step 3: Conclusion on Fever Trigger
The periodic liberation of haemozoin at each synchronous cycle of RBC lysis corresponds precisely to the periodic fever spikes every 3 to 4 days.

Final Answer: Haemozoin released upon the rupture of red blood cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q13 - Sequence of Plasmodium development in human host

questiontext.text: Following inoculation into the human bloodstream via the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, what is the initial site of asexual multiplication for Plasmodium sporozoites?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Inoculation Stage
The infective stage of Plasmodium introduced by the mosquito vector into the human body is the motile sporozoite, carried rapidly via the circulation.

Step 2: Pre-erythrocytic Hepatic Multiplication
Sporozoites preferentially target and penetrate hepatic parenchyma cells (hepatocytes), where they undergo primary asexual schizogony to generate thousands of merozoites before bursting into the bloodstream to attack erythrocytes.

Step 3: Sequence Determination
Asexual reproduction in the liver strictly precedes any invasion, reproduction, or lysis in circulating red blood cells.

Final Answer: Parenchymal liver cells prior to attacking red blood cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q14 - Anatomical sites of gamete fertilization and sporozoite storage

questiontext.text: In the complex digenetic life cycle of Plasmodium, where do fertilization of gametes and subsequent storage of mature sporozoites occur within the mosquito host?

Step 1: Uptake of Gametocytes
A female Anopheles mosquito ingests sexual stages (male and female gametocytes) along with a blood meal from an infected human host.

Step 2: Site of Syngamy and Maturation
Gamete fertilization and zygote maturation proceed within the lumen of the mosquito gut. The resulting motile ookinete develops into an oocyst on the stomach wall, generating mature sporozoites that escape into the hemocoel.

Step 3: Migration to Vector Reservoir
These mature infectious sporozoites actively migrate to and are stored within the mosquito salivary glands, ready for inoculation during subsequent feeding.

Final Answer: Fertilization takes place in the gut, and sporozoites are stored in salivary glands

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q15 - Pathology and transmission of Entamoeba histolytica

questiontext.text: Entamoeba histolytica colonizes which anatomical compartment of the human digestive tract, and what are the hallmark clinical manifestations of amoebic dysentery?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Habitat of the Protozoan
Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite that establishes infection within the mucosal crypts and wall of the human large intestine.

Step 2: Clinical Symptomatology
Invasion and ulceration of the large intestinal mucosa result in amoebic dysentery characterized by abdominal pain, severe cramps, constipation alternating with loose motions, and stools containing excess mucus and blood clots.

Houseflies act as mechanical carriers transporting cysts from fecal matter to foodstuffs, making contaminated water and food the primary infection sources.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q16 - Pathology and modes of transmission of Ascaris

questiontext.text: Which combination of clinical symptoms and transmission route is characteristic of ascariasis caused by the intestinal roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Parasite Identity and Habitat
Ascaris lumbricoides is a prevalent helminthic endoparasite residing in the lumen of the human small intestine.

Step 2: Pathological Manifestations
Clinical ascariasis features internal bleeding, persistent muscular pain, low-grade fever, anemia due to nutritional theft, and mechanical blockage of the intestinal passage under heavy worm burdens.

Embryonated eggs excreted in human feces contaminate surrounding soil, irrigation water, and crop vegetation, infecting healthy individuals via unwashed vegetables, fruits, or water.

The adult worms reside for years in the lymphatic vessels, typically of the lower extremities and genital tract, provoking chronic obstructive inflammation and massive lymphedema transmitted through the bite of female mosquito vectors.

Controlling insect vectors involves eliminating their breeding habitats or utilizing natural predators that consume developmental stages of mosquitoes.

The introduction of larvivorous fishes, specifically Gambusia, into standing water bodies and ponds effectively suppresses vector populations because these fish actively feed on mosquito larvae.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q21 - Primary physical barriers in innate defense

questiontext.text: Which anatomical structures constitute the primary physical barriers preventing the initial entry of microorganisms into the human body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of Innate Immunity
Innate immunity provides non-specific frontline defenses operational from birth, divided into physical, physiological, cellular, and cytokine barriers.

Step 2: Characterization of Physical Barriers
The intact keratinized skin covering the external body surface is the foremost barrier against microbial penetration, complemented by the mucus coating of epithelial linings along the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and urogenital tracts that physically traps invading microbes.

Step 3: Distinction from Secretions and Cells
Gastric acid and tears represent physiological fluids, while neutrophils and macrophages constitute cellular barriers.

Final Answer: Skin and the mucus coating of internal epithelial tracts

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q22 - Chemical secretions acting as physiological barriers

questiontext.text: Which set of secretions exemplifies the physiological barriers of innate immunity that impede microbial growth and colonization?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism of Physiological Defense
Physiological barriers involve biochemical conditions, secretions, and enzymes that inhibit microbial proliferation without direct cellular engulfment.

Step 2: Evaluation of Physiological Agents
The highly acidic gastric juice (low pH) in the stomach, antibacterial enzymes in saliva, and lysozyme in tears actively prevent microbial growth and colonisation across vulnerable mucosal surfaces.

Step 3: Distinction from Cellular and Physical Defenses
Epithelial membranes represent physical barriers, while phagocytic leukocytes represent cellular defenses.

questiontext.text: Which specific group of leukocytes and tissue-resident cells serves as the cellular barrier of innate immunity capable of phagocytosing and destroying microbes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Components of Cellular Defense
Cellular barriers comprise non-specific white blood cells that identify, engulf, or lyse foreign invaders immediately upon encounter.

Step 2: Identification of Participating Cell Types
This barrier includes polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNL-neutrophils), circulating monocytes, natural killer (NK) lymphocytes in the blood, and tissue-resident macrophages, all capable of phagocytosing pathogens.

Step 3: Exclusion of Acquired Effector Cells
B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes constitute adaptive antigen-specific humoral and cell-mediated immunity rather than innate cellular barriers.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q24 - Role and source of interferons in cytokine defense

questiontext.text: What is the functional mechanism of cytokine barriers in innate immunity, particularly through the action of interferons?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Origin of Interferons
When host cells are infected by viruses, they synthesize and release specialised regulatory glycoproteins known as interferons.

Step 2: Mechanism of Paracrine Protection
Interferons diffuse locally to bind receptors on neighboring uninfected cells, inducing an antiviral state that blocks viral transcription and translation, thereby protecting non-infected cells from subsequent infection.

Step 3: Scope of Action
Interferons do not directly lyse bacteria or neutralize bacterial toxins; their primary evolutionary role is antiviral resistance.

Final Answer: Proteins secreted by virus-infected cells to protect uninfected cells from viral infection

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q25 - Characteristics of primary and anamnestic immune responses

questiontext.text: Why does a secondary encounter with the same pathogen elicit a highly intensified (anamnestic) response compared to the initial primary response?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Primary Immune Response Kinetics
During an initial encounter with a novel pathogen, the immune system takes time to recognize the antigen and expand effector clones, yielding a slow, low-intensity primary response.

Step 2: Basis of the Anamnestic Response
Acquired immunity generates long-lived memory B-cells and memory T-cells during the primary response. Upon subsequent re-exposure to the identical pathogen, these memory cells rapidly activate, producing a massive and swift secondary response.

Step 3: Distinction from Innate Defenses
This intensified response depends strictly on immunological memory of the first encounter rather than non-specific physical barriers.

Final Answer: The body retains immunological memory of the initial encounter, enabling rapid activation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q26 - Polypeptide chain composition of an antibody molecule

questiontext.text: What is the basic polypeptide architecture of an immunoglobulin monomer, and why is it conventionally designated as \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{L}_2\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural Composition of Immunoglobulins
An antibody molecule is a Y-shaped glycoprotein composed of four distinct polypeptide chains.

Step 2: Chain Identity and Configuration
It consists of two identical smaller polypeptide chains called light (L) chains and two identical longer polypeptide chains termed heavy (H) chains linked together by interchain disulfide bonds, establishing the formula \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{L}_2\).

Step 3: Functional Loci
Each arm of the monomer displays a variable domain providing an antigen-binding site at the amino-terminal ends.

Final Answer: It possesses two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q27 - Cellular mediation of humoral and cell-mediated immunity

questiontext.text: Acquired immunity comprises humoral and cell-mediated branches. Which lymphocytes are responsible for antibody secretion and cell-mediated immunity (CMI), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Division of Adaptive Immunity
Adaptive immunity operates via two functionally distinct lymphocyte populations: B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes.

Step 2: Functional Specialization
B-lymphocytes produce and secrete soluble immunoglobulins into blood and lymph, constituting the humoral immune response. T-lymphocytes do not secrete circulating antibodies; instead, they assist B-cells and directly execute cell-mediated immunity (CMI).

Step 3: Core Distinction
Humoral immunity is antibody-driven via B-cells, whereas CMI is orchestrated and executed by T-cells.

Final Answer: B-lymphocytes mediate humoral immunity while T-lymphocytes mediate cell-mediated immunity

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q28 - Immunological mechanism responsible for allograft rejection

questiontext.text: When human organ transplants fail due to graft rejection despite blood group matching, which immunological mechanism and cell type are primarily responsible for recognizing the foreign tissue as 'non-self'?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism of Histocompatibility Recognition
The mammalian immune system possesses the ability to discriminate between self-tissues and non-self allogeneic tissues based on major histocompatibility antigens.

Step 2: Effector Pathway in Rejection
Cell-mediated immunity (CMI), driven by T-lymphocytes, actively recognizes foreign histocompatibility antigens present on the grafted organ, initiating cellular cytotoxicity that results in allograft destruction.

Step 3: Clinical Management
To suppress this T-cell mediated response, transplant recipients require rigorous tissue matching and lifelong administration of immunosuppressive drugs.

Final Answer: Cell-mediated immune response executed by T-lymphocytes

Infection by lethal toxins like Clostridium tetani tetanospasmin or snake neurotoxins requires immediate neutralization before endogenous active immune defenses can develop.

Patients are directly injected with preformed antibodies or antitoxins (antivenom), providing instantaneous passive neutralization of circulating toxins.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q32 - Immunoglobulin and chemical mediators involved in allergy

questiontext.text: Allergy is an exaggerated immune response to environmental antigens. Which specific class of immunoglobulins is produced, and which chemicals are released from mast cells during an allergic reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Immunological Mechanism of Type I Hypersensitivity
Exposure to environmental allergens such as pollen grains, dust mites, or animal dander stimulates plasma cells to synthesize excessive amounts of IgE immunoglobulins.

Step 2: Effector Phase and Mediator Release
These IgE antibodies bind high-affinity receptors on tissue mast cells. Subsequent cross-linking triggers mast cell degranulation, releasing vasoactive mediators including histamine and serotonin.

Step 3: Pathological Consequence
Histamine and serotonin cause vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, bronchoconstriction, and typical symptoms like sneezing, watery eyes, and dyspnea.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q33 - Pharmacological agents alleviating acute allergy symptoms

questiontext.text: Which combination of pharmaceutical drugs is clinically administered to rapidly reduce acute symptoms during severe allergic reactions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Pathophysiology of Allergic Manifestations
Allergic symptoms such as bronchospasm, mucosal edema, and hypotensive vascular dilation stem from sudden systemic release of mast cell mediators.

Step 2: Pharmacological Countermeasures
Antihistamines directly block histamine H1-receptors; adrenaline rapidly reverses bronchoconstriction and supports vascular tone; corticosteroids suppress underlying inflammatory cascades.

Step 3: Synthesis of Drug Classes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q34 - Pathological basis of autoimmunity and classic example

questiontext.text: What defines an autoimmune disease at the cellular level, and which prevalent human condition serves as a classic textbook example of such an abnormality?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Tolerance and Self-Non-Self Discrimination
Higher vertebrates evolved memory-based acquired immunity capable of distinguishing foreign antigenic molecules from self-antigens.

Step 2: Pathology of Autoimmunity
When immune tolerance fails due to genetic defects or aberrant triggers, the immune system launches an attack against the host's own tissues, creating autoimmune pathology.

Step 3: Canonical Human Example
Rheumatoid arthritis is a classic autoimmune disease where chronic immune-mediated inflammation damages synovial joints and surrounding tissues.

Final Answer: Failure to distinguish self from non-self, exemplified by rheumatoid arthritis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q35 - Distinction between primary and secondary lymphoid organs

questiontext.text: How do primary lymphoid organs functionally differ from secondary lymphoid organs in the development and execution of the human immune response?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Role of Primary Lymphoid Organs
Primary lymphoid organs (bone marrow and thymus) represent the developmental nurseries where immature progenitor lymphocytes differentiate, proliferate, and mature into immunocompetent, antigen-sensitive T-cells and B-cells.

Step 2: Role of Secondary Lymphoid Organs
Secondary lymphoid organs (spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix) provide specialized microenvironments for mature lymphocytes to interact with trapped foreign antigens and clonally proliferate into effector cells.

Step 3: Key Functional Divergence
Primary organs foster lymphocyte maturation in an antigen-independent environment, whereas secondary organs host antigen encounters and effector immune responses.

Final Answer: Primary organs facilitate lymphocyte maturation into antigen-sensitive cells, while secondary organs provide sites for antigen interaction

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q36 - Anatomical location and age-related involution of thymus

questiontext.text: Where is the thymus gland anatomically situated in the human body, and what characteristic morphological change does it undergo from birth through puberty?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Anatomical Position of Thymus
The thymus is a bilobed lymphoid organ situated in the thoracic cavity near the heart and deep to the breastbone (sternum).

Step 2: Age-Related Involution
The gland is relatively large at birth, continues to function prominently in early life to mature T-lymphocytes, and then progressively atrophies with age, reducing to a very small size by the onset of puberty.

Step 3: Clinical Significance
This developmental involution correlates with the gradual decline in naive T-lymphocyte generation during adult life.

Final Answer: Located near the heart beneath the breastbone, it progressively decreases in size with age

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q37 - Comparative physiological roles of spleen and lymph nodes

questiontext.text: What are the distinct physiological roles performed by the spleen and lymph nodes within the secondary lymphoid network?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Functional Profile of the Spleen
The spleen is a large bean-shaped abdominal organ packed with lymphocytes and phagocytes. It functions primarily as a hemodynamic filter trapping blood-borne microorganisms and serves as a major reservoir for erythrocytes.

Step 2: Functional Profile of Lymph Nodes
Lymph nodes are small solid capsules distributed along the lymphatic system that trap antigens and particulate matter entering lymph and tissue fluid, activating localized resident lymphocytes.

Step 3: Comparative Synthesis
The spleen filters circulating blood, whereas lymph nodes filter interstitial lymph fluid.

Final Answer: The spleen acts as a blood filter and erythrocyte reservoir, while lymph nodes trap antigens from lymph and tissue fluid

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q38 - Proportion of lymphoid tissue constituted by MALT

questiontext.text: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), located within the epithelial lining of the major respiratory, digestive, and urogenital tracts, constitutes approximately what percentage of all lymphoid tissue in the human body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition and Distribution of MALT
MALT comprises unencapsulated aggregates of lymphoid tissue strategically embedded within mucosal linings exposed to external environments (bronchial, gastrointestinal, and urogenital).

Step 2: Quantitative Contribution
Because of the vast surface area of these visceral tracts, MALT constitutes approximately 50 percent of the total lymphoid tissue in the human body.

Step 3: Confirmation of Standard Value
This 50 percent proportion reflects the critical evolutionary requirement for mucosal surface immune vigilance.

Final Answer: 50 per cent

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q39 - Structural and genetic characteristics of HIV

questiontext.text: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), the causative pathogen of Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS), belongs to which viral group and possesses which type of genome?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Taxonomic Classification of HIV
HIV is classified under the genus Lentivirus, a member of the family of retroviruses.

Step 2: Structural and Genetic Makeup
Retroviruses are characterized by an outer lipid-protein envelope enclosing a viral core that houses a single-stranded RNA genome along with reverse transcriptase enzymes.

Step 3: Pathogenic Strategy
Upon infecting susceptible host cells, this RNA template is transcribed into complementary DNA for genomic integration.

Final Answer: Retrovirus group, with an envelope enclosing an RNA genome

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q40 - Role of macrophages as viral factories

questiontext.text: Following initial infection, how do host macrophages function during HIV replication without being immediately destroyed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Entry and Reverse Transcription
Upon entering the body, HIV particles target macrophages, where the viral single-stranded RNA is reverse transcribed into complementary viral DNA by the enzyme reverse transcriptase.

Step 2: Genomic Integration and Viral Factory
This viral DNA integrates into the host cell nucleus, directing the macrophage to continuously transcribe and translate viral progeny. The macrophage survives while continuously releasing new virions, thereby acting as an 'HIV factory'.

Step 3: Comparative Cellular Fate
Unlike helper T-lymphocytes which undergo progressive lysis and depletion, macrophages persist as sustained viral reservoirs.

Final Answer: Viral RNA forms viral DNA via reverse transcriptase, enabling the macrophage to continuously produce and release virions while surviving

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q41 - Mechanism of immunodeficiency in AIDS pathogenesis

questiontext.text: What specific cellular mechanism is responsible for the profound immunodeficiency seen in symptomatic AIDS patients?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Targeting of Helper T-Lymphocytes
Simultaneously with macrophage infection, HIV virions bind and enter CD4-bearing helper T-lymphocytes (\(\mathrm{T}_\mathrm{H}\)).

Step 2: Progressive Lysis and Depletion
The virus replicates inside helper T-cells, and the release of progeny virions lyses the host cells. Repeated rounds of infection and lysis cause a progressive decline in helper T-lymphocyte numbers in the blood.

Step 3: Loss of Immunocompetence
Because helper T-cells are essential for orchestrating both humoral and cell-mediated defenses, their depletion leaves the host unable to protect against opportunistic microbes like Mycobacterium, Toxoplasma, fungi, and viruses.

Final Answer: Progressive decrease in helper T-lymphocytes due to repeated viral replication and cell lysis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q42 - Cellular aberrations distinguishing malignant tumors

questiontext.text: Which fundamental regulatory cellular property is lost in neoplastic cells, and what dangerous characteristic allows malignant tumors to establish secondary growths at distant sites?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Loss of Cellular Regulation
Normal non-transformed somatic cells exhibit contact inhibition, a property whereby physical contact with adjacent cells arrests further cell division. Cancer cells lose contact inhibition and continue uncontrolled proliferation.

Step 2: Invasion and Dissemination
Malignant tumor cells actively invade surrounding tissues. Cells sloughing off into the bloodstream or lymphatic channels lodge at distant anatomical locations, initiating secondary tumor foci through the process of metastasis.

Step 3: Evaluation of Neoplastic Traits
The breakdown of contact inhibition initiates tumorigenesis, and metastasis represents the most aggressive and feared characteristic of malignant neoplasms.

Final Answer: Loss of contact inhibition leads to uncontrolled division, and metastasis spreads cells to distant organs

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q43 - Classification of carcinogens and cellular oncogene activation

questiontext.text: How do ionizing radiations, non-ionizing radiations, and chemical carcinogens induce oncogenic transformation, and what pre-existing cellular genes are implicated?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of Carcinogenic Agents
Neoplastic transformation is triggered by physical mutagens (ionizing X-rays and gamma rays, non-ionizing UV), chemical mutagens (e.g., tobacco smoke chemical carcinogens), and biological oncogenic viruses.

Step 2: Activation of Endogenous Genes
Normal cells carry evolutionary conserved cellular oncogenes (c-onc) or proto-oncogenes. Exposure to carcinogens causes DNA damage or mutational activation, converting these benign proto-oncogenes into active oncogenes that drive neoplastic growth.

Step 3: Synthesis of Cellular Events
Carcinogens produce structural DNA changes or deregulate cellular proto-oncogenes, disrupting cell division control.

Final Answer: They cause DNA damage or activate cellular proto-oncogenes (c-onc) into active oncogenes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q44 - Role of alpha-interferon in cancer immunotherapy

questiontext.text: Why are cancer patients therapeutically administered biological response modifiers such as \(\alpha\)-interferon as part of their comprehensive oncological treatment?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Immune Evasion by Tumor Cells
Neoplastic cells frequently evade immune surveillance and destruction by downregulating recognition antigens or suppressing surrounding lymphoid activity.

Step 2: Mechanism of Biological Response Modifiers
Exogenously administered \(\alpha\)-interferon acts as a biological response modifier that stimulates the host's innate and adaptive immune machinery, including natural killer cells and cytotoxic lymphocytes, enabling them to recognize and destroy malignant cells.

Step 3: Integration into Cancer Therapy
Immunotherapy using \(\alpha\)-interferon supplements surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy by restoring active antitumor immunity.

Final Answer: It activates the patient's immune system to overcome immune evasion and destroy tumor cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q45 - Chemical derivation, receptors, and physiological action of heroin

questiontext.text: Heroin (commonly known as smack) is chemically diacetylmorphine. How is it synthesized from raw poppy extract, which receptors does it bind, and what is its primary systemic physiological effect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Source and Chemical Derivation
Morphine is an alkaloid extracted from the latex of the opium poppy Papaver somniferum. Acetylation of morphine's hydroxyl groups yields diacetylmorphine, a white, odorless, bitter crystalline compound known as heroin.

Step 2: Receptor Target and Physiological Effect
Heroin binds specific opioid receptors located in the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract. Functionally, it acts as a depressant that significantly slows down bodily functions.

Step 3: Rejection of Contradictory Actions
It does not stimulate dopamine transport or act as a cardiovascular stimulant; its primary clinical signature is central nervous depression.

Final Answer: Acetylation of morphine; binds CNS and GI opioid receptors, acting as a depressant that slows body functions

Step 1: Botanical Origin of Cannabinoids
Natural cannabinoids are harvested from the inflorescences of the Indian hemp plant Cannabis sativa. Combinations of the flower tops, leaves, and resin are processed to produce marijuana, hashish, charas, and ganja.

Step 2: Receptor Location and Physiological Action
Cannabinoids interact with specific cannabinoid receptors localized principally within the brain. Upon inhalation or oral ingestion, their most prominent and immediate systemic physiological effects occur on the cardiovascular system.

Step 3: Clinical and Toxicological Relevance
These compounds alter heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiovascular hemodynamics, leading to their abuse and detection in athletic doping panels.

questiontext.text: Cocaine (coca alkaloid) interferes with the transport of which neurotransmitter, and what other plants are well known for potent hallucinogenic properties?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism of Action of Cocaine
Cocaine, extracted from the South American shrub Erythroxylum coca, competitively inhibits the reuptake transporter of dopamine at central synapses, leading to dopamine accumulation, intense central nervous stimulation, euphoria, and increased energy.

Step 2: Excess Dosage and Hallucinogenic Flora
Excessive doses of cocaine induce vivid hallucinations. Other botanical species containing potent hallucinogenic alkaloids include Atropa belladonna and Datura.

Cocaine is a CNS stimulant, while morphine is a depressant; Datura and Atropa belladonna are classical hallucinogenic Solanaceae.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MCQ_Q48 - Endocrine side effects of anabolic steroids

questiontext.text: The illicit use of anabolic steroids by sportspersons to enhance muscle bulk and aggressive performance induces which specific adverse side effects in females and males?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Physiological Basis of Steroid Abuse
Sportspersons abuse synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroids to promote protein synthesis, muscle hypertrophy, and competitive aggression beyond physiological limits.

Step 2: Side Effects in Females
In females, excessive anabolic steroids induce masculinization, deepening of the voice, abnormal menstrual cycles, hirsutism (excessive body and facial hair), and clitoral enlargement.

Step 3: Side Effects in Males and Adolescents
In males, exogenous steroids cause feedback suppression of the pituitary-gonadal axis, resulting in testicular atrophy, reduced sperm production, gynecomastia (breast enlargement), acne, and premature closure of long-bone epiphyses causing stunted growth in adolescents.

Final Answer: Masculinization and clitoral enlargement in females; testicular reduction and breast enlargement in males

Step 2: Evaluation of the Second Proposition
The statement regarding the IARI research facility is factually correct. The School of Cytogenetics and Radiation Research established at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute provided the technological platform for developing high-yielding rice cultivars, including scented Basmati.

questiontext.text:

Statement I: Early medical systems like Hippocrates and Indian Ayurveda asserted that health was a state where there was a balance of certain humors, associating blackbile with fevers.

Statement II: William Harvey proved the good humor hypothesis of health by demonstrating elevated body temperature in persons with blackbile using pure reflective thought.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the First Proposition
The statement describing early medical doctrines is historically accurate. The ancient humor hypothesis asserted that health reflected a balance among bodily humors, positing that individuals with blackbile had hot personalities predisposed to fevers.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Second Proposition
The statement attributing the proof of this hypothesis to William Harvey is incorrect. Harvey disproved the good humor hypothesis through the experimental discovery of blood circulation and the objective demonstration of normal body temperatures in individuals with blackbile using a thermometer.

Step 3: Synthesis and Conclusion
Evaluating both statements reveals that the first proposition is valid, whereas the second proposition is invalid.

Final Answer: The statement describing the historical humor hypothesis is correct, whereas the statement claiming William Harvey proved the hypothesis is incorrect.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Second Proposition
The statement delineating adaptive immune effector branches is incorrect. Humoral immunity is mediated by soluble antibodies produced by B-lymphocytes, whereas cell-mediated immunity (CMI) is mediated directly by T-lymphocytes.

Evaluating both statements reveals that the first proposition is correct, whereas the second proposition is inverted and incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_S2_Q11 - Differentiation between natural passive and artificial passive immunity

The statement regarding colostrum is immunologically accurate. Neonates lack mature adaptive defenses; secretory IgA absorbed from maternal colostrum confers natural passive mucosal protection.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Second Proposition
The statement concerning tetanus antitoxin is incorrect. Antitoxin preparations contain preformed exogenous antibodies against tetanospasmin; delivering ready-made antibodies constitutes passive immunization, not active immunity.

Step 3: Synthesis and Conclusion
Evaluating both statements shows that the first proposition is valid, whereas the second proposition misidentifies the immunological category.

Final Answer: The statement regarding colostrum conferring passive immunity is correct, whereas the statement regarding tetanus antitoxin providing active immunity is incorrect.

The statement regarding rheumatoid arthritis is correct. Rheumatoid arthritis represents an autoimmune disease characterized by aberrant immune recognition and chronic destruction of self synovial tissues.

Step 3: Synthesis and Conclusion
Evaluating both statements confirms that the first proposition is false, while the second proposition is true.

Final Answer: The statement regarding allergic mediators is incorrect, whereas the statement regarding rheumatoid arthritis as an autoimmune disorder is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_S3_Q02 - Pathological features of typhoid and pneumonia infections

questiontext.text:

The proposition regarding Salmonella typhi is factually correct. The bacterium enters the small intestine via contaminated food and water, migrates systemically, and can cause intestinal perforation and fatality in severe clinical cases.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Second Proposition
The proposition regarding pneumonia pathogens is factually correct. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae infect pulmonary alveoli, which become filled with inflammatory exudate and fluid, impairing oxygen exchange.

The proposition regarding dysentery, plague, and diphtheria is factually incorrect. Dysentery, plague, and diphtheria are bacterial infections, not viral disorders, and their transmission involves ingested contaminants, vectors, or respiratory droplets rather than purely skin contact.

Step 4: Synthesis and Conclusion
Evaluation demonstrates that the propositions detailing Salmonella typhi and alveolar pneumonia are accurate, whereas the taxonomic classification of dysentery, plague, and diphtheria as viral ailments is inaccurate.

Final Answer: Only the first and second propositions are correct.

questiontext.text:

The proposition regarding the infective stage of Plasmodium is factually correct. Sporozoites stored within the salivary glands of the female Anopheles mosquito are inoculated into the human host during a blood meal.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Second Proposition
The proposition regarding parasitic hepatic reproduction is factually incorrect. In humans, sporozoites initially enter liver cells (hepatocytes) and multiply asexually via schizogony before attacking erythrocytes; they do not reproduce by binary fission inside leukocytes.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Third Proposition
The proposition regarding haemozoin release is factually correct. The synchronized rupture of erythrocytic schizonts releases toxic haemozoin pigment crystals into systemic circulation, inducing rigors, intense chills, and high fever.

Step 4: Synthesis and Conclusion
Analysis shows that the propositions detailing sporozoite inoculation and haemozoin-mediated fevers are correct, whereas the claim denying hepatocyte infection is incorrect.

Final Answer: Only the first and third propositions are correct.

The proposition regarding cannabinoid actions is factually correct. Phytocannabinoids bind to endogenous cannabinoid receptors primarily situated in the brain and exert well-documented physiological actions on the cardiovascular system.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Second Proposition
The proposition regarding cocaine action is factually correct. Erythroxylum coca alkaloid (cocaine) blocks the reuptake transport of dopamine at synaptic junctions, producing central nervous system stimulation, euphoria, and heightened motor energy.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Third Proposition
The proposition regarding morphine pharmacology is factually incorrect. Morphine is a powerful narcotic analgesic and central nervous system depressant (not a stimulant); it relieves severe postoperative pain and slows physiological bodily functions.

Step 4: Synthesis and Conclusion
Analysis confirms that the receptor actions of cannabinoids and dopamine inhibition by cocaine are described accurately, whereas classifying morphine as a central stimulant is incorrect.

Final Answer: Only the first and second propositions are correct.
